slides: Open by framing Chapter 1 as a question about legitimacy in Euclidean geometry. Euclidean figures look familiar, but this lecture asks what must be constructed, assumed, or proved before a figure can carry a proof.

This route slide gives students the lecture map before details arrive. Emphasize that the chapter moves from Euclid I-1 to hidden assumptions, then to proof dependencies, the pentagon, and modern triangle-center results. Treat each stop as a proof license.

Define the local vocabulary for the lecture slowly, since these words will recur on later slides. A straightedge operation creates the line through two already available points, while a compass operation creates a circle with constructed center and copied radius.

Use Euclid I-1 as the first stress test because it is small enough to see completely. The two circles encode the two copied radii, and the chosen intersection point becomes the third vertex. Existence is the key checkpoint.

This slide turns the previous picture into a formal certificate. Walk through the rows as a dependency chain: begin with the segment, draw two circles, take an intersection, and join the new point to the endpoints.

Here the lecture pauses on a subtle point: a diagram may show two curves crossing, but the formal system still needs a principle allowing the intersection point. The rational plane example is a useful warning because the unit equilateral triangle wants a height involving sqrt(3), which does not live among rational coordinates.

This is the chapter's methodological pivot. Euclid's postulates and common notions supply part of the proof engine, but practice also depends on diagrammatic assumptions such as order, continuity, and superposition. That distinction will matter later.

The slide contrasts two kinds of equality that students often merge too quickly. Equal by construction means the equality follows because a compass radius was copied or a line was defined by two points; equal by theorem means a previous proposition or common notion is doing the work.

Use this slide to show why the pentagon is more than a five-sided drawing. The construction is governed by a special isosceles triangle with angles 36, 72, and 72 degrees. The angle pattern drives the proof.

This is the algebraic core of the pentagon section. The diagonal-to-side ratio is phi, and phi satisfies phi squared equals phi plus one. The point is not to derive the identity line by line here; it is to show how exact algebra certifies the equality of the five chord lengths.

This slide compares a correct pentagon with a nearly correct one. The nudged vertex is visually plausible, which makes it pedagogically useful: the certificate residuals detect the error before the eye insists something is wrong.

The lecture now shifts from classical constructions to newer triangle results while preserving the same checking habit. Midpoints, medians, altitudes, and perpendicular bisectors are all constructed objects with incidence claims. Each center hides a theorem.

Use the Euler line as a compact example of modern Euclidean structure. In a non-equilateral triangle, the centroid, circumcenter, and orthocenter line up, and their spacing has a fixed relation. The ratio is part of the claim.

The nine-point circle is a good capstone because it collects several constructions into one invariant object. The midpoints of sides, feet of altitudes, and midpoints from vertices to the orthocenter all lie on a single circle.

This slide names common failure modes that appear throughout the chapter. The first is trusting visual intersection, the second is treating a copied length as if it were copied without a compass step, and the third is forgetting orientation or betweenness.

Pose the exercise as a design task rather than a rote proof. Students choose a favorite Euclidean construction and write down its certificate before drawing it. Residuals make weak steps visible before the diagram persuades.

Close by returning to the chapter question. Euclid's geometry is powerful because it links construction, assumption, and proof in a repeatable order. The computational language in the notebook does not replace Euclid; it makes the same obligations visible enough to audit.
